{"notes": "VISIT 1 (left at 1:00). Early observations only. I don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build yet.

Table state: one curved line of about 14 dominoes runs from the start toward the lower left. All are connected to the start and none look stray or detached. It looks like the start of the top line, but I can't say whose work it is. No belly or tail pieces were visible yet.

Leo: Set direction fast. Chose the fish, took the top line from the nose and assigned Maya the belly. Clear, decisive leadership. Still to check: does he hand the pad to Priya on time, and does he accept Tom's offer of help on the far half?

Priya: Backed the plan right away and restated assignments so the team shared one picture. Took the tail, with a plan to sketch the fork after Leo. Her best moment was noticing that the belly line starts at the nose and so only falls once the top line reaches it. That is a useful dependency insight. Collaboration and leadership look strong. Still to see: her build output.

Tom: Supportive. Offered to back up Leo on the top line, with a specific offer to take the far half, and plans to check joints for breaks. Good quality-minded, collaborative instincts. Watch whether he actually builds or just inspects.

Maya: Said nothing while I was there, and Leo assigned her the belly. No evidence yet for or against her. Check next visit whether she's working, stuck, or waiting on the top line. Don't penalize her quiet start.

Next visit: look for gaps in the line, whether the belly is progressing, and whether the tail is started."}

{"notes": "VISIT 2 (left at 2:30). I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build.

Table: the single top line now runs from the start across to about x=9, roughly 40 dominoes (up from about 14). Every piece is connected and none are stray or pale, so the build is clean. Still not visible: any belly line, tail or fork. Timing is a concern, with 7.5 minutes left and the belly and tail not yet started.

Leo: Still laying the top line, with about a dozen left at 2:00. He set a clear boundary with Tom ('don't redo what's down', then check joints at the head). He handed the sketch to Priya and told her to start the fork from the end of a line. Good direction and delegation. Watch whether he finishes the head and moves people onto the belly in time.

Tom: Proactive. He announced he was jumping on the top line round the head and offered to shift if they collided. His 1:45 move came before Leo's reply, so he slightly overlapped, but he adapted. Good communication. I can't tell whether he actually placed anything. Check next visit whether he is building or inspecting.

Priya: Gave an accurate status update (connected, all falls from the start to the head). She is coordinating a plan to meet in the middle on the belly and checking joints in the meantime. Strong collaboration and leadership, but still no visible build output and no fork yet. Check on the tail.

Maya: Silent again while I was there. The belly isn't visible, so I have no direct evidence of her work either way. Priya's plan assumes she is on it. Don't penalise her yet, but ask her directly next visit whether she is blocked."}

{"notes": "VISIT 3 (left at 5:15). I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build.

Table: the full fish outline now exists (top line, head, belly, tail fork). But only about 15 dominoes, from the start up the right side to about (22, 11.5), are connected. There's a visible gap just past that point, and everything beyond it is pale. If time ran out now, almost nothing would fall. The gap is at the belly/tail joint, which is exactly the joint Priya asked Tom to check. Next visit: confirm that gap is closed.

Maya: Finally spoke, with a clear, cooperative reply at 5:00 ('a few more dominoes, then I stop at the end of my line'). That answers my earlier worry about silence. She is reliable on handoff, but I haven't seen her place anything, and I can't tell whether the gap is on her side.

Priya: Led the plan. She told Maya where to stop, said she would take the tail from Maya's line end, and delegated the joint check to Tom. Clear leadership and collaboration. Her claim that she is building is unverified, and she told me earlier everything was connected, which the picture doesn't support. Ask her about the gap.

Tom: Given a specific task (check the Priya/Maya joint). I didn't hear a reply or see him do it. His earlier proactivity was good. Check whether he has actually verified the joint.

Leo: Not seen or heard this visit. Earlier direction and delegation were good. Ask whether the head joints are verified and who owns fixing the break."}

{"notes": "VISIT 4 (left at 6:00). I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build.

Table: The earlier gap at the belly/tail joint is now closed. The top line, head, belly and lower tail fork all show as connected to the start, so the main outline would fall. Remaining problem: the upper tail fin (from about (22.8, 8.3) up to (27, 4)) is still pale and disconnected, roughly 10 dominoes. Next visit: confirm that last link is made and the fin is chained on. I can't tell who fixed the joint, so I won't credit anyone for it.

Priya: Kept leading. She told Leo to hold off, said her stroke would do the bridge, and asked Tom to check her/Maya's joint. Clear and collaborative, but her message and Leo's overlapped, and her earlier 'everything connected' claim was wrong. Ask who owns the upper tail fin.

Leo: Responded promptly and cooperatively, agreeing to meet Priya at the join and nudge his last dominoes into line. Nudging placed dominoes near a live chain is a risk, though it worked out. Ask him to confirm the head joints and what he plans for the tail fin.

Tom: Still no reply or visible follow-up on Priya's second request to check the joint. Earlier proactivity was good, but this visit gave me nothing to rate. Ask directly what he checked.

Maya: Not seen or heard this visit. Earlier handoff was reliable. No new evidence; ask whether she is helping with the fin."}

{"notes": "VISIT 5 (left at 7:15). I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build.

Table: The upper tail fin is now dark and chained on from about (23, 9) up to (27, 4), so every main section looks connected to the start. Two pale dominoes remain at the fin/top-line joint, around (22.7-23, 8.2). They don't seem to be carrying the chain, but I should check them. Next visit: confirm they are harmless or dark, and that nobody nudges anything near the live chain during the final minutes.

Maya: Checked the fin herself and gave an accurate status (about a dozen pale dominoes). She kept clear of Leo's bridge and asked for a verification check, which was good judgment and collaboration. Reliable again. Ask what else she is checking.

Leo: Said the bridge into the upper tail is down, and the fin is now dark. He asked others to stay clear and is verifying it himself, which shows ownership and care. I can't confirm he physically placed it. Ask him what he found when he checked, and about the two pale dominoes at the joint.

Priya: Not seen or heard this visit. Earlier she led clearly but wrongly claimed everything was connected. No new evidence. Ask whether she accepts that Leo owned the fin.

Tom: Silent for a second visit. No answer to Priya's request to check the joint. Earlier proactivity was good, but I have nothing recent to rate. Ask directly what he has checked and done."}

{"notes": "VISIT 6 (left at 9:00). I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for the physical build. Table: the chain looks dark from the start through the lower tail, the body, and the upper fin out to about (27, 4). Two pale dominoes remain at the fin/top-line joint, around (22.7-23, 8.2). They look like they aren't carrying the chain, but nobody confirmed that, and the push is about to run. Watch for whether the fall passes through the joint cleanly. Nobody was touching anything at 9:00.

Leo: Said 'it's all dark from the start' and told everyone to stay clear. That's slightly overstated, since two pale dominoes are still visible at the joint. He never answered my earlier question about them. Good ownership of the fin and a sensible hands-off call, but a small accuracy gap in his status report. Ask what he knew about those two.

Priya: Reported the lower tail dark, then stepped back and invited Leo to shout if anything was pale. Good delegation, though she relied on Leo's word rather than checking. Her earlier wrong 'all connected' claim makes this a pattern worth noting. Her leadership is visible, her verification less so.

Maya: Said 'looks great from here' and kept hands off. Her last visit's checking was stronger. This time she accepted the group view without flagging the pale pair. Fine collaboration, less independent verification.

Tom: Spoke for the first time in a while, but only to say 'looks great' and promise to shout if he saw anything pale. Pale dominoes were visible and he didn't shout. I still have no evidence of what he checked or did. Ask him directly in the review."}

{"self_assessment":"Impact: I chose the animal and the design. I proposed a large fish because its outline reads as a fish on its own, and I sketched it on the pad with the start at the nose, a top line and a belly line, and a forked tail. I laid the start domino and the whole top line, which carries the fall from the start round the head. By the end, about 123 of the 125 standing dominoes were connected to the start.

Execution: I laid the top line from the start round the head and added dominoes to round the tight nose turn so the fall could pass into the belly. When the top line and belly were falling toward the start, I bridged from the end of the belly line up into the top line so the fall could go round the whole fish. I then closed the gap where the upper tail meets the top line. I inspected the nose joint and the upper tail join several times, and nudged the dominoes that sat off the line until the picture was dark from the start. I stopped touching things once it was connected, to avoid bumping the table.

Collaboration: I split the work early. Maya took the belly line, Priya the tail, and Tom was asked to check joints and help with the belly. I asked people to stay clear of a spot while I worked on a joint, and I told the table when the top line had reached the nose so the belly could start there. In the last minutes I kept everyone hands off so nothing was knocked.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first minute, assigned strokes, and kept the team coordinated on one sketch. I kept attention on what the start would actually knock over. That caught the fall-direction problem at the join and the pale upper tail, and the team fixed both before the push. We finished with time to spare and a connected fish.","my_share_percent":40}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took ownership of the tail section, the last stretch of the fish. I sketched it on the pad and laid it with several builds (stroke 3), running from where the belly line ended out through the forked tail. The tail makes the outline read as a fish. When I finished, the lower tail was dark all the way out, and the start was tracing through nearly all of the standing dominoes.

Execution: I inspected the joints early, at about the 1:30, 2:00, 2:45 and 4:00 marks, so I knew the state of the table before I built. I sketched my stroke so it began on an existing line, as the pad guidelines require. I then laid it in short builds and checked the result with two close inspections near the end. Once the lines were connected, I kept my hands off to avoid bumping anything.

Collaboration: I worked to keep the table coordinated. I told people which part I was taking, asked Maya to stop the belly at a clear point so my stretch could catch on, and asked Tom to check the joint where our lines met. I flagged the jammed spot under the nose. I stayed off the head and the top line, which others were building, to avoid doubling up. I also called for hands-off near the end.

Leadership: I kept the group updated, gave short status reports, and set clear handoffs. I helped keep the mood upbeat as the clock ran down. We finished with the fish connected from the start. I believe my tail work and my coordination were an important part of that result.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the belly line, stroke 2, which is the whole lower outline of the fish from the nose round to the middle of the bottom. I laid about 40 dominoes, all connected, and handed the end off cleanly so the lower tail could catch on from it. This stretch was a large share of the fish's silhouette and kept the lower body readable as a fish. By the final check the whole fish was dark from the start.

Execution: I picked one piece of work and stayed on it steadily from about 3:30 to 5:15, tracing the stroke straight from the pad so the shape matched the sketch. I stopped at the agreed point in the middle of the bottom so the next stretch could join. I also stood one domino back up. Later I inspected the upper tail join twice, found about a dozen unconnected dominoes, and reported it clearly so the team could close the gap. I confirmed it looked dark afterwards.

Collaboration: I told the table early that I had the belly stroke, so nobody doubled up on it. I asked Tom not to lay it from the tail end, which avoided a messy joint, and pointed him to joint checks instead. I coordinated the handoff point with Priya. In the final stretch I kept my hands off the dominoes and encouraged everyone else to do the same, so nothing got bumped before the push.

Leadership: I kept ownership of my stroke without needing direction, and I made clear calls on who works where. I also used my inspection to give the table accurate information on what was still disconnected, so effort went where it was needed. I supported the fish plan Leo proposed and moved it forward quickly. I believe my share of the table's result was about a quarter, given how much of the fish was built by teammates.", "my_share_percent": 27}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: My main contribution was quality checking. I inspected the joints throughout the build: the nose turn, the belly and tail meeting point, and the upper tail join. I stood two dominoes back up, including a jammed one just under the nose that I nudged into line. The nose turn carries the fall from the top line into the belly, so that fix mattered. I kept the table's pale/dark status in view, which helped the team see the whole fish was connected to the start. The fish was all dark before the push.

Execution: I worked in short, targeted passes of inspect, fix, and re-inspect, rather than laying large strokes myself. I looked at problem areas repeatedly through the second half. I stayed off the dip and the belly when teammates asked, so no domino was laid twice and the table had fewer chances of a bump. I kept my hands off once everything was dark.

Collaboration: I offered help to Leo and Maya early, and when they asked me to hold back I did so promptly and redirected to joint checks. I posted clear updates, such as the nudge under the nose, and told people I would step in if anything went pale. I backed the plan to build the fish in sections: top line, belly, tail.

Leadership: I backed the fish idea from the start and kept the team's attention on connectivity, which was the real risk. Late on, I reinforced the hands-off discipline so nothing got bumped before the push. I was willing to take whichever job was most useful, including the far end of the top line and the last stretch of the belly, and I made those offers openly.

Overall, my work was in verification and joint care, which supported a connected fish that fell as a single run.", "my_share_percent": 15}
